m: Om. I meditate on her seated on a jewelled throne, dark of limb, listening to the parrot recite, one foot placed on a lotus, wearing the crescent moon, playing the vina, a garland of white water-lilies bound on her, her bodice shining in a measured way, dressed in jewelled cloth,
Matangi, holding a conch and a cup, delighting in sweet honey-wine, her brow shining with a painted mark. Om. The seer said:
Commanded, the daityas then went forth, with Chanda and Munda at their head, equipped with a fourfold army and with weapons raised.
They saw the Goddess standing there with a slight smile, on her lion, on a great golden peak of the lord of mountains.
Seeing her, they made ready to seize her. Some came near her with bows drawn and swords in hand.
Then Ambika became exceedingly angry toward those enemies. In her anger her face became the colour of ink.
From the flat of her forehead, bent with a frown, Kali came forth at once, her mouth gaping, bearing sword and noose.
She carried a strange skull-topped club, wore a garland of human heads, was dressed in a tiger skin, and was exceedingly terrible with dried flesh.
Her mouth was very wide, her lolling tongue was frightful, her eyes were sunken and red, and her roar filled the mouths of the directions.
She fell upon them with speed, striking down the great asuras, and in that army of the gods' enemies she devoured its force.
Seizing with one hand the elephants, together with those who guarded their rear, those who held the goads, the fighters, and the bells, she flung them into her mouth.
In the same way she threw into her mouth a warrior with his horses, and a chariot with its charioteer, and crushed them terribly with her teeth.
She seized one by the hair and another by the neck. She stamped on another with her foot, and crushed yet another against her chest.
The weapons and great missiles that the asuras released she caught in her mouth in her rage, and ground them with her teeth.
She crushed that whole army of the powerful, evil-minded asuras, devoured some, and struck others.
Some asuras were slain by the sword, some struck by the skull-club, and some, hit by the tips of her teeth, went to destruction.
In a moment that entire army of asuras was struck down. Seeing this, Chanda rushed at Kali, who was exceedingly terrible.
The great asura covered that terrible-eyed one with very dreadful showers of arrows, and Munda covered her with discs thrown by the thousand.
Those many discs, entering her mouth, looked like many orbs of the sun entering the belly of a cloud.
Then Kali laughed, exceedingly enraged, roaring a terrible roar, her mouth gaping, her dreadful teeth flashing.
The Goddess rose upon her great lion and rushed at Chanda. Seizing him by the hair, she cut off his head with her sword.
Then Munda rushed at her, seeing Chanda struck down. In her rage she felled him too to the ground, struck by the sword.
Seeing the army that remained after the slaughter, seeing Chanda struck down, and seeing Munda of very great valour, the rest fled in fear to the directions.
Kali, taking the head of Chanda and also the head of Munda, approached Chandika and spoke, her words mixed with a fierce loud laugh.
I have brought you here Chanda and Munda, two great beasts of the sacrifice. In the sacrifice of battle you yourself will slay Shumbha and Nishumbha.
The seer said:
Seeing the two great asuras, Chanda and Munda, brought to her, Chandika, the gracious one, spoke to Kali a playful word.
Because you have come bringing Chanda and Munda, you will be famed in the world as the Goddess Chamunda.
